questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Near miss after a fix
questions.question: A nurse at a regional hospital catches a lab result routed to the wrong patient's chart, and the lab fixes the routing rule the same day. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Reassess the misrouting scenario using the near miss
options.B: Close the incident and keep the scenario's existing rating
options.C: Have the lab manager assess a second check on results
options.D: Escalate the near miss to the board's risk committee

questions.key_concept: Near misses are likelihood evidence; after any event, reassess the linked risk scenario before anyone chooses new controls.
questions.pre_read: Notice what happened, what was lost and what has already been fixed.
questions.correct_explanation: A near miss is likelihood evidence: it shows the misrouting scenario can happen and that a nurse was the last barrier. With the fault contained, the risk practitioner reassesses the scenario's likelihood and impact using the event, so the risk owner can decide whether the fix is enough. Weighing a second check may help, but it studies a control before the risk itself is reassessed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the fault is fixed. But fixing the cause closes the ticket, not the risk; the near miss is new evidence the rating must reflect.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since a second check could prevent repeats. But it studies a control before the risk is reassessed, and choosing the response belongs to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because patient safety is serious. But the board sets appetite; one near miss is first analyzed and reported through the risk owner, not escalated unassessed.

tips: Eliminate: B closes the incident while leaving the rating blind to new evidence, and D sends one unassessed near miss to the board, which sets appetite rather than reviewing single events.
Final two: A beats C because the near miss must first update the scenario's rating; only then can the risk owner judge whether another control is worth it.
Exam cue: once an incident or near miss is contained, the first risk move is to update the scenario and its rating, even when the fault is already fixed.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Gradual AI performance change
questions.question: Over six months, a bank's loan-triage AI model has gradually routed more sound applications to manual review, raising handling costs, but no incident was logged. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Monitor the scenario's manual review rate with a new KRI
options.B: Have the data science team retrain the model on recent loans
options.C: Log the drift as a tuning task for data scientists to assess
options.D: Record the drift as a risk event against the AI scenario

questions.key_concept: Model drift is a risk event; record it against the AI risk scenario and reassess before anyone chooses a fix.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed, over what period, and what it has cost so far.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift is a risk event even when nothing fails: rising manual review is a real cost that builds gradually. The risk practitioner first records it against the AI triage scenario, so likelihood and impact are reassessed and the business owner can decide on a response, such as retraining with the data science lead as control owner. A KRI on the review rate is useful, but it comes after that reassessment, which sets its threshold.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since a KRI tracks the trend. But six months of drift is already evidence; record it against the scenario and reassess, then set KRI thresholds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining is a common fix for drift. But it acts before the risk is assessed, and the business owner, not the risk practitioner, chooses the treatment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because data scientists tune models. But filing drift as tuning work keeps a business risk away from its owner and out of the register.

tips: Eliminate: B retrains the model before the risk is assessed, a treatment the business owner chooses, and C files drift as tuning work, keeping a business risk out of the register.
Final two: D beats A because six months of drift is already a risk event to record and reassess; a KRI on the review rate comes after, with its threshold set by that reassessment.
Exam cue: AI bias and drift are risk events with a business owner. Record and assess them like any other event before anyone fixes the model.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Threat source classification
questions.question: A risk analyst at a logistics firm records a scenario in which a database administrator runs a cleanup script on production instead of the test database. How should the analyst BEST classify the threat source?

options.A: Adversarial
options.B: Structural
options.C: Accidental
options.D: Environmental

questions.key_concept: NIST SP 800-30 classes everyday errors by staff, including privileged administrators, as accidental threat sources, separate from adversarial insiders.
questions.pre_read: Notice who acted, what they intended and what actually failed.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-30 Table D-2 classes erroneous actions by people doing their everyday jobs, including privileged users and administrators, as accidental threat sources. The administrator had no intent to harm; they ran the right script on the wrong database. Adversarial sources, privileged insiders included, act on purpose, so intent rather than access level separates the two.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since privileged insiders appear under adversarial sources. But adversarial means intent to harm; an administrator's honest mistake is accidental.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a database is software. But structural sources are equipment or software failing on their own; here the software worked and a person erred.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because production infrastructure was harmed. But environmental sources are natural disasters and outside infrastructure outages, not actions by the enterprise's staff.

tips: Eliminate: B needs equipment or software to fail on its own, and D covers disasters and outside infrastructure outages; here a person ran a script.
Final two: C beats A because the taxonomy separates sources by intent. Privileged insiders are adversarial only when they mean harm; an administrator's honest error is accidental.

Exam cue: classify a threat source by intent and cause, not access level. Staff errors are accidental whatever their privileges, and their likelihood comes from error history, not adversary capability.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix D Table D-2 (Taxonomy of Threat Sources: adversarial, accidental, structural and environmental)

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. New AI threat intelligence
questions.question: A sector sharing group warns that applicants hide instructions in resumes to manipulate AI screening tools, and a recruitment firm's assistant summarizes uploaded resumes. What should the firm's risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Suspend resume uploads until the security team tests the assistant
options.B: Assess the prompt injection risk to the screening assistant
options.C: Rely on existing email and web filters to block the instructions
options.D: Assess the threat as low likelihood based on internal history

questions.key_concept: New AI threats such as indirect prompt injection are first recorded and assessed as scenarios with the business owner, before treatment.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the attack text would enter the system and who relies on the service.
questions.correct_explanation: Threat intelligence is an input to analysis, not a decision. The risk practitioner first assesses the indirect prompt injection risk to the screening assistant and records it with the risk owner, who then chooses the response. Suspending uploads might prove sensible, but deciding on it before analysis puts treatment ahead of assessment and takes the call from the owner, who must also weigh hiring delays.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since suspension closes the attack path. But it chooses a treatment before the risk is assessed, and that decision belongs to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because filters screen content. But hidden instructions are ordinary text in approved documents; email and web filters cannot tell them from normal resume content.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the firm's own history is direct evidence. But a new technique has little history; credible sector intelligence about the same kind of tool raises likelihood.

tips: Eliminate: C expects perimeter filters to spot instructions that arrive as ordinary text, and D judges likelihood from internal history when credible sector intelligence covers the same kind of tool.
Final two: B beats A because a new threat is first assessed with its owner; suspending uploads is a treatment the owner chooses afterward.
Exam cue: when intelligence reports a new AI threat, record and assess the risk with its business owner before anyone switches features off.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Severity scores in the register
questions.question: A bank's vulnerability team proposes copying each finding's CVSS Base score straight into the risk register as its risk rating. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Use the score as one input beside asset impact and exposure
options.B: Accept the proposal as a consistent industry-standard rating
options.C: Use each finding's environment-adjusted CVSS score as its rating
options.D: Rate each finding scored above 7.0 as a high register risk

questions.key_concept: A CVSS score is a severity input; a risk rating also needs the asset's business impact, its exposure and the likelihood of exploitation.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a CVSS score measures and what a register rating is used to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: A CVSS score, even fully adjusted, measures the technical severity of a flaw, and the CVSS specification calls it an input to risk assessment. Risk also depends on what the asset supports, how reachable it is and the business impact of exploitation, so the risk practitioner uses the score as one input to the scenario rating. An environment-adjusted score is a better input, but still a severity score, not a business risk rating.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because CVSS is widely used and consistent. But a standard severity score still describes the flaw, not the business harm if the asset is exploited.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since environmental and threat metrics add context. But an adjusted score is still a severity score; the rating also needs the business impact of exploitation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a threshold looks consistent. But a fixed cutoff ranks findings by severity alone, with no view of which business process each asset supports.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a standard severity score as business risk, and D sets register ratings by a severity cutoff with no view of what each asset supports.
Final two: A beats C because environmental and threat metrics refine severity, but business impact still has to be combined with the score to rate risk.
Exam cue: CVSS rates the flaw, not the risk. Expect the key to combine the score with asset value, exposure and business impact.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Control test finding
questions.question: Control testing at a hospital finds pharmacists can approve their own dosage-limit changes in the pharmacy system, and only one pharmacist works the night shift. How should the risk practitioner BEST handle this finding?

options.A: Refer it to internal audit to track as a compliance issue
options.B: Log it with IT as a pharmacy system configuration defect
options.C: Record it as a vulnerability in the medication error scenario
options.D: Ask the pharmacy manager to remove the self-approval right

questions.key_concept: Control deficiencies are vulnerabilities; record them against the affected risk scenarios and re-rate before treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice what kind of weakness the test found and how the hospital is staffed.
questions.correct_explanation: A control deficiency is a vulnerability: self-approval of dosage limits weakens protection against medication errors just as a missing patch weakens a server. The risk practitioner records it in the medication error scenario, so the scenario is re-rated and the risk owner can weigh responses. Removing the right looks obvious, but with one pharmacist on nights it could block urgent changes, a trade-off the owner must weigh.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because control test results are shared with audit. But the weakness changes a business risk now; tracking it only as compliance keeps it out of the risk register.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the right is set in the system. But self-approval is a process weakness; filing it as an IT defect keeps it from the risk owner and the register.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice, since the gap looks urgent. But removal could stop the lone night pharmacist making urgent changes; the owner weighs that once the scenario is re-rated.

tips: Eliminate: A routes a live business risk to audit tracking instead of the register, and B files a process weakness as an IT configuration defect.

Final two: C beats D because the obvious fix carries its own night-shift safety cost; re-rating the scenario lets the risk owner weigh removal against options such as a next-morning independent review.
Exam cue: a failed or missing control is a vulnerability. Record it against the scenarios it weakens before anyone picks the fix.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Generic register entry
questions.question: A university's risk register lists 'cyberattack' as one high-rated scenario with no further detail, and owners cannot agree on controls. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Re-rate the scenario using the latest threat intelligence
options.B: Ask IT to list the controls that reduce cyberattack risk
options.C: Split it into scenarios naming actor, asset and impact
options.D: Run a tabletop exercise on the scenario with business owners

questions.key_concept: A risk scenario must name the actor, event, asset, timing and consequence; generic entries cannot be rated, owned or linked to controls.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the register entry actually says and why the owners are stuck.
questions.correct_explanation: A scenario as broad as 'cyberattack' cannot be rated or tied to controls, which is why owners disagree. The risk practitioner first splits it into specific scenarios, each naming the actor, the asset affected and the business impact, so each one can be rated and owned. A tabletop exercise is valuable later, but exercising a vague scenario produces a vague discussion; specificity comes first.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fresh intelligence improves ratings. But a scenario as vague as 'cyberattack' cannot be rated meaningfully, whatever the data; it must first name an actor, asset and impact.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls are what owners argue about. But a control list for a vague threat cannot show which controls matter for which assets.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice, since exercises test scenarios with the business. But a scenario this vague gives the exercise nothing concrete to test; define specific scenarios first.

tips: Eliminate: A re-rates an entry too vague to rate, and B lists controls before the scenario shows which assets and events they must address.
Final two: C beats D because a tabletop exercise needs a concrete scenario to test; splitting the generic entry into specific scenarios has to come first.
Exam cue: when owners cannot agree on a risk, check whether the scenario is specific: actor, event, asset, time and consequence.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Exercise finding
questions.question: At a retailer's tabletop exercise, store operations leaders say the top risk scenario misses that card payments fail when the loyalty service is down. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Update the scenario to include the loyalty service dependency
options.B: Keep the scenario as written by the risk team's experts
options.C: Ask the IT director to decouple payments from the loyalty service
options.D: Note the comment in the exercise minutes for later review

questions.key_concept: Tabletop findings and business-owner input revise scenarios and the register before any treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice who raised the gap and what they know about the business that others may not.
questions.correct_explanation: Tabletop exercises exist to expose gaps like this one, and the people who run the business know its dependencies best. The risk practitioner updates the scenario to include the loyalty dependency, so it is re-rated with store operations and the register shows the exposure with an owner. Asking IT to decouple the systems jumps to a fix before the revised scenario is assessed, and the risk owner, not the practitioner, chooses the response.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk team built the scenario carefully. But business leaders know the operational dependencies; a scenario they show to be incomplete must change.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since the dependency causes the harm. But it orders a fix before the revised scenario is assessed, and the response belongs to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the minutes capture it. But a finding that lives only in minutes is easily lost; it must become a register update with an owner.

tips: Eliminate: B overrides the business leaders who know the dependency, and D leaves an exercise finding in minutes rather than turning it into a tracked register update.
Final two: A beats C because the gap first updates the scenario and its rating; decoupling the systems is a response the risk owner may choose afterward.
Exam cue: a tabletop finding should change the scenario and the register, with an owner. Look for the option that turns the gap into a tracked update.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Starting a new assessment
questions.question: Before a new warehouse robotics system goes live, a logistics firm's COO asks the risk practitioner for a risk assessment. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Identify threats and vulnerabilities in the robotics system
options.B: Agree the purpose, scope and rating criteria with the COO
options.C: Request the vendor's security test results for the robots
options.D: Weigh the system's risk against appetite for the launch

questions.key_concept: A risk assessment begins by agreeing purpose, scope, assumptions and rating criteria, before identifying threats or rating risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much of the request has been defined so far.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-30 starts every assessment with preparation: the purpose, the scope, the assumptions and the risk criteria. Without them the risk practitioner cannot tell which threats matter or how to rate them, and the COO may get answers to the wrong question. Identifying threats and vulnerabilities is the core of the work, but it belongs to the conduct step, after scope and criteria are agreed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since threats and vulnerabilities are central. But without an agreed scope and criteria, the team cannot tell which ones matter or how to rate them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendor tests are useful evidence. But they are one information source for the conduct step, not a substitute for preparing the assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because appetite drives the launch decision. But risk cannot be compared with appetite before it is identified and analyzed; evaluation comes last.

tips: Eliminate: C treats one vendor input as the start of the assessment, and D compares risk with appetite before any risk has been analyzed.
Final two: B beats A because preparation comes before the conduct step; scope and criteria decide which threats and vulnerabilities are worth listing and how to rate them.
Exam cue: for the FIRST step of a new assessment, look for purpose, scope, context or criteria before any threat list or rating.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Change after approval
questions.question: Eight months after a bank approved its risk assessment of a card-processing provider, the provider moves processing to a new subcontractor. What is the BEST action for the bank's risk practitioner?

options.A: Reassess the provider at the next scheduled annual review
options.B: Update the assessment to reflect the new subcontractor
options.C: Ask the risk owner to add a subcontractor clause to the contract
options.D: Discard the old assessment and start a new one from scratch

questions.key_concept: Risk assessments are maintained: a material change triggers an update and a briefing to the owner before new treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed since the assessment was approved, and what has not.
questions.correct_explanation: An assessment stays live. The maintain step in NIST SP 800-30 monitors risk factors and updates the assessment when they change, and a new subcontractor changes who handles cardholder data. The risk practitioner updates the affected parts and communicates the result to the risk owner, who decides on any response. A contract clause may well follow, but asking for one now treats a risk that has not yet been reassessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reviews run on a cycle. But a material change to who processes the data triggers reassessment now, not at the next annual date.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since a subcontractor clause is a common fix. But it picks a treatment before the changed risk is reassessed; the owner should choose with the update in hand.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the old view is out of date. But most of the assessment still holds; maintaining it means updating the affected parts, not repeating all the work.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for the calendar despite a material change, and D repeats the whole assessment when only the changed factors need updating.
Final two: B beats C because the changed risk is reassessed first; a contract clause is one response the owner may choose after seeing the update.
Exam cue: a significant change to a system, supplier or threat triggers an update to the assessment now, followed by communication to the risk owner.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). BIA and risk assessment
questions.question: A city council's continuity manager argues that the new BIA already ranks the council's top risks, so no separate risk assessment is needed. Which of the following is the PRIMARY flaw in this view?

options.A: A BIA does not identify which processes are critical
options.B: A BIA studies threats but not the vulnerabilities they exploit
options.C: A BIA leaves recovery objectives for the IT team to set
options.D: A BIA assumes the disruption occurs and ignores likelihood

questions.key_concept: A BIA measures impact over time and ignores likelihood, so it complements a risk assessment but cannot replace it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a BIA produces and what a ranking of risks requires.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA measures how harm grows over time if a process stops, assuming the disruption happens. It never estimates how likely each disruption is, so it cannot rank risks on its own; a risk assessment combines likelihood with impact, using the BIA's impact data. Missing vulnerability analysis is the runner-up, but vulnerabilities only feed likelihood: a BIA starts from the outage and, whatever threats it notes, never estimates how likely each disruption is.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because criticality sounds like risk. But identifying critical processes is the BIA's main output; the missing piece is how likely each disruption is.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since threats and vulnerabilities drive risk. But a BIA starts from the outage and measures impact; whatever threats it notes, it never rates likelihood, which ranking risks needs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recovery objectives sound technical. But a BIA gathers them from business owners; the gap in this view is likelihood, not who sets objectives.

tips: Eliminate: A denies the BIA's core output, critical processes, and C misplaces who sets recovery objectives, which a BIA gathers from business owners.
Final two: D beats B because a BIA starts from the disruption and measures impact over time; whatever threats it notes, it never rates likelihood, which ranking risks requires.
Exam cue: a BIA is impact over time, assuming the event happens. A risk assessment is likelihood and impact together. Neither replaces the other.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Recovery objective for an AI service
questions.question: A hospital's IT team sets a 48-hour RTO for its AI sepsis-alert service because that matches the vendor's standard restore time. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the RTO based on the vendor's recovery capability
options.B: Ask IT to buy the vendor's faster recovery service tier
options.C: Set a matching 48-hour RPO for the sepsis-alert service data
options.D: Ask clinical leads how long care can safely run without alerts

questions.key_concept: RTO and RPO are set by business owners from BIA results, AI services included, not by IT or vendor capability.
questions.pre_read: Notice who set the RTO and what it was based on.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery objectives come from the business through the BIA, not from what a vendor offers. The risk practitioner first asks the clinical leads how long care can run safely without sepsis alerts, which sets the maximum tolerable outage the RTO must fit within. Buying a faster tier might follow, but spending before the business tolerance is known could buy too little recovery, or far too much.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows its platform. But a vendor's restore time shows what is offered, not how long clinicians can work safely without alerts.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since faster recovery looks safer. But it commits money before the business tolerance is known; the clinical leads' answer decides what recovery is needed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because matching numbers look tidy. But RPO measures tolerable data loss, not restore time; it is set separately, from how much data the process can afford to lose.

tips: Eliminate: A lets the vendor's offer set the objective, and C confuses RPO, which measures tolerable data loss, with RTO, which measures restore time.
Final two: D beats B because the business tolerance must be known before recovery is bought; the clinical leads' answer sets what the RTO must achieve.
Exam cue: when IT or a vendor sets an RTO or RPO, the first move is to get the process owner's tolerance through the BIA.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Entry status after approval
questions.question: A risk practitioner finds that a retailer's register shows payment page skimming as closed because a script-integrity tool was approved for deployment next quarter. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate register entry?

options.A: Closed, with the approved response on record
options.B: Closed, with a reminder to confirm deployment
options.C: In treatment, rated on the controls in place today
options.D: In treatment, left unrated until the tool is deployed

questions.key_concept: A register entry stays open, rated on current controls, until the planned response is implemented and shown to work.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has been approved and what is actually deployed.
questions.correct_explanation: Register status must follow evidence. A tool approved but not yet deployed reduces nothing, so the entry is in treatment and rated on the controls actually in place, which is its current risk. Leaving it unrated until deployment is the runner-up: it reopens the entry, but for a whole quarter owners and the risk profile would show no rating for an exposure that exists today.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approval is a real milestone. But an approved plan is not a working control; the risk stays at its current level until deployment.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it tracks deployment. But the closed status still misreports today's exposure for months; status must reflect what is in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice, since the entry is reopened. But an unrated entry drops out of comparisons with appetite; current risk is rated now, on today's controls.

tips: Eliminate: A counts an approved plan as a working control, and B keeps a closed status that misreports today's exposure until deployment.
Final two: C beats D because an open risk still needs a current rating; leaving it unrated until deployment hides today's exposure from the people who decide.
Exam cue: register status and rating follow evidence. Planned or approved controls never close an entry, and an open entry is rated now on the controls in place.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Rolling up unit ratings
questions.question: A supermarket chain's risk practitioner finds four regions each rate an outage of their shared ordering platform as low. Which of the following BEST represents this risk in the enterprise risk profile?

options.A: A low rating, matching the four regional ratings
options.B: One group scenario rated on combined impact
options.C: The average of the four regions' separate ratings
options.D: Four regional scenarios linked to the shared platform

questions.key_concept: Aggregation can turn several low local risks into one significant enterprise risk when units share an asset or weakness.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the four regions have in common and how each rating was set.
questions.correct_explanation: When units share one platform, a single outage hits all four regions at once, so four low ratings can hide a significant group exposure. The profile needs one group scenario, rated on its combined impact against the enterprise scale, before it is compared with appetite. Linking the four regional entries is the runner-up: it shows the connection but leaves four lows, so the combined exposure is never rated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the regions agree. But each region rated only its own slice; one shared outage hits all four at once, so the combined impact is larger.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because averaging looks like normalization. But an average of four low ratings stays low and still misses the combined impact of one shared failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice, since links show the shared platform. But four entries each rated low still hide the group exposure; the combined impact must be rated as one scenario.

tips: Eliminate: A treats four local lows as a low group risk, and C averages the ratings, which keeps the shared outage's combined impact hidden.
Final two: B beats D because the profile must rate the combined impact; linking four low regional entries shows the connection but never rates the group exposure.
Exam cue: when several units share one asset or weakness, aggregate their entries into one enterprise scenario and rate the combined impact.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Annualized loss calculation
questions.question: An e-commerce firm's $600,000 checkout platform loses 25% of its value in each outage, and outages occur about once every three years. What is the risk practitioner's BEST estimate of the ALE?

options.A: About $50,000 a year
options.B: About $150,000 a year
options.C: About $200,000 a year
options.D: About $450,000 a year

questions.key_concept: ALE equals SLE times ARO, where SLE is asset value times exposure factor and ARO is the expected number of events per year.
questions.pre_read: Separate the loss from one outage from how often outages happen.
questions.correct_explanation: SLE is asset value times exposure factor: $600,000 times 0.25 is $150,000. An event once every three years gives an ARO of about 0.33. ALE is SLE times ARO, so about $50,000 a year. The runner-up, $150,000, is the SLE: the loss from a single outage before the annual rate is applied. ALE is the figure to compare with a control's yearly cost.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: this is the SLE, the loss from one outage. It leaves out the annual rate of occurrence of one outage every three years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it divides by three. But it skips the 25% exposure factor, treating the whole platform value as lost in each outage.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting if the three years is multiplied in. But the ARO is one third a year, so the SLE is divided by three, not multiplied.

tips: Eliminate: D multiplies by three when an event every three years gives an ARO of one third, and C skips the 25% exposure factor.
Final two: A beats B because B is the SLE for one outage; multiplying it by the ARO of one third gives the yearly expectation.
Exam cue: SLE equals asset value times exposure factor, ARO is events per year, and ALE equals SLE times ARO. Once every N years means an ARO of one over N.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Funding a failover
questions.question: A clinic chain's records outage has an $80,000 ALE, and a $30,000-a-year failover would cut it to $20,000. Which of the following is the BEST basis for the risk practitioner's advice to the records owner?

options.A: The $30,000 cost against the remaining $20,000 ALE
options.B: Five years of cost against the $80,000 ALE
options.C: The 75% cut in yearly expected loss from outages
options.D: The $60,000 ALE reduction against the $30,000 cost

questions.key_concept: A control is cost-justified when the yearly ALE reduction exceeds its yearly cost; percentages and mismatched time periods mislead, and the risk owner decides.
questions.pre_read: Line up each figure with the period it covers before comparing them.
questions.correct_explanation: Cost-benefit compares the yearly cut in ALE with the control's yearly cost: $80,000 minus $20,000 is a $60,000 reduction against a $30,000 cost, a net benefit of $30,000 a year. On that basis the risk practitioner recommends the failover, and the records owner decides. A 75% cut sounds persuasive, but a percentage alone cannot show whether the saving exceeds the cost.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because $30,000 is more than $20,000. But $20,000 is the loss that would remain; the benefit is the $60,000 reduction, double the cost.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a multi-year view looks prudent. But it sets five years of spending against one year of expected loss; compare both on a yearly basis.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since the cut is real. But a percentage ignores cost; a 75% cut could still cost more than the loss it removes.

tips: Eliminate: A compares cost with the loss that would remain instead of the reduction, and B sets five years of cost against one year of expected loss.
Final two: D beats C because cost-benefit weighs the yearly loss reduction against the yearly cost; a percentage cut alone cannot show the control is worth buying.
Exam cue: control value is ALE before minus ALE after, compared with yearly cost. Then check who decides: the risk owner, not the practitioner.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Request for an exact figure
questions.question: A payments start-up's board asks the risk practitioner for one exact ALE for fraud on a new product with no loss history. Which of the following is the BEST response?

options.A: A single exact ALE from expert estimates
options.B: An annual loss range from expert estimates
options.C: A deferral until three years of loss data exists
options.D: A high qualitative rating until loss data exists

questions.key_concept: Quantitative results must match input quality; with thin data, give ranges and stated uncertainty rather than a falsely precise figure.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much data stands behind the number the board wants.
questions.correct_explanation: With no loss history, a single exact ALE would carry false precision and could mislead the board. The risk practitioner gives a loss range built from several calibrated expert estimates, states the uncertainty and assumptions, and shows how better data would narrow it. A single figure meets the request literally, but NIST SP 800-30 warns that subjective inputs buried in a quantitative result significantly lessen its rigor.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since it gives the board what it asked for. But one exact figure from thin data looks precise without being reliable, which would mislead the board.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the data is thin. But decisions cannot wait years; ranges from calibrated estimates give usable analysis now, with the uncertainty made clear.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because missing data feels risky. But a rating must reflect estimated likelihood and impact; defaulting to high because data is thin distorts priorities.

tips: Eliminate: C withholds analysis the board needs now, and D rates the risk by its data gaps instead of by estimated likelihood and impact.
Final two: B beats A because a range with stated uncertainty is honest about thin data, while one exact figure from the same estimates gives the board false precision.
Exam cue: when data is poor, prefer ranges with stated assumptions, or honest qualitative estimates, over exact-looking numbers. Precision must match the inputs.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Rating compared with appetite
questions.question: A water utility's risk practitioner is preparing advice on whether its control system intrusion scenario is within risk appetite today. Which of the following ratings is MOST appropriate to compare with appetite?

options.A: Current risk, crediting only controls implemented and working
options.B: Residual risk projected once next year's planned controls go live
options.C: Inherent risk, before the utility's controls are counted
options.D: Current risk reported by peer utilities in a sector benchmark

questions.key_concept: Today's exposure is current risk, crediting only implemented, working controls; future residual (target) risk, projected for planned responses, judges the plan, not today's position.
questions.pre_read: Notice what decision the advice supports and the point in time it refers to.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether the utility is within appetite today depends on current risk, which the ISACA Glossary defines as counting actions already taken but not those proposed. A projection counting next year's planned controls is what the Glossary's risk response entry calls future residual risk: it shows whether the plan will be enough, not today's exposure. If current risk is above appetite, the practitioner takes treatment options to the risk owner.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since the plan matters. But planned controls reduce nothing yet; projected residual risk shows whether the plan is enough, not whether the utility is within appetite today.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because inherent risk shows the full threat. But it leaves out controls already working, so comparing it with appetite overstates the need for treatment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because peers face similar threats. But appetite is compared with this utility's own exposure; a peer figure reflects other controls and assets, not the utility's current risk.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves out controls that already work, overstating the need for treatment, and D swaps the utility's own exposure for a peer benchmark.
Final two: A beats B because only implemented, working controls count today; a projection with planned controls is future residual risk, used to judge the plan.

Exam cue: compare today's risk, counting only implemented, working controls, with appetite; ISACA may call it current or residual risk. A projection with planned controls judges the plan; inherent risk only shows reliance on controls.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Untested control credit
questions.question: A university's register rates research data theft as low residual risk because laptop encryption was installed two years ago, though it has not been tested since installation. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Keep the low rating based on the owner's confirmation
options.B: Re-rate the scenario at its inherent level until it is tested
options.C: Ask IT for coverage reports showing the encryption is active
options.D: Recommend replacing the tool with a newer encryption product

questions.key_concept: Residual ratings credit controls only for demonstrated effectiveness; obtain evidence before keeping or changing the rating.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the low rating relies on and when that control was last checked.
questions.correct_explanation: A control earns credit in residual risk only for what evidence shows it does, and existence is not effectiveness. The risk practitioner first asks IT, which answers for the encryption as control owner, for evidence such as device coverage reports and recovery-key checks. Re-rating to inherent is the runner-up: the low rating is unsupported, but inherent strips credit from every control, and a quick evidence check should come before any re-rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner vouches for it. But installed is not effective: encryption may be disabled or missing from devices, and only evidence earns a low rating.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since the low rating is unsupported. But inherent counts no controls at all; ask for the evidence first, then re-rate on what the encryption actually does.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because newer tools sound stronger. But nobody yet knows whether the current tool is failing; replacing it before getting evidence treats an unanalyzed gap.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the owner's word as proof the tool works, and D replaces a control before anyone knows whether it is failing.
Final two: C beats B because evidence comes before any re-rating; dropping to inherent strips credit from every control, while coverage reports show what the encryption really does.
Exam cue: when a rating relies on an untested control, the first step is evidence of design and operating effectiveness, then re-rating.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Residual above appetite
questions.question: After two new controls went live, a city council's ransomware scenario still has residual risk above the appetite its elected council approved. What is the risk practitioner's BEST next step?

options.A: Sign off the residual risk as reduced as far as practical
options.B: Report the large drop from inherent risk as an acceptable result
options.C: Ask the IT control owner to deploy a third ransomware control
options.D: Present further treatment options and costs to the risk owner

questions.key_concept: When residual risk exceeds appetite, the practitioner presents costed treatment options and the risk owner chooses the response.
questions.pre_read: Notice where residual risk sits against appetite after the new controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Residual risk above appetite needs more treatment, but the choice belongs to the risk owner. The risk practitioner presents options, such as further mitigation, transfer or changing the activity, with their costs and target ratings, so the owner can decide. Asking IT to deploy a third control may end up as one of those options, but directing it skips the owner's decision and the cost-benefit comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because real effort has been made. But risk above appetite needs more treatment or a decision by the level that set appetite; acceptance is never the practitioner's call.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk did fall. But decisions compare residual risk with appetite, not with inherent risk; a large reduction can still leave risk above appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since IT is accountable for the controls. But it picks the treatment for the owner; options and costs go to the risk owner, who chooses the response.

tips: Eliminate: A has the practitioner sign off risk that exceeds appetite, and B judges success against inherent risk rather than against appetite.
Final two: D beats C because the risk owner chooses the treatment from costed options; directing IT to add a control takes that decision from the owner.
Exam cue: residual risk above appetite means more treatment, chosen by the risk owner from options the practitioner prepares. Watch for options where the practitioner decides.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Peer outage reports
questions.question: A risk analyst learns that three peer airlines lost a day of flights when a crew-scheduling platform that the analyst's airline also uses failed. How should the analyst BEST use these peer events?

options.A: As a direct measure of the airline's own exposure
options.B: As rating input, adjusted for local exposure
options.C: As a trigger to replace the scheduling platform
options.D: As background until the airline has its own loss

questions.key_concept: External loss events inform a scenario's rating, adjusted for the enterprise's own exposure and controls before the rating changes.
questions.pre_read: Notice whose losses these were and what the airline shares with them.
questions.correct_explanation: Peer events show the platform can fail and how much harm follows, so they are real evidence for the airline's vendor outage scenario. The analyst feeds them into the rating after adjusting for local exposure, such as the airline's contract terms, fallback procedures and size. Taking the peers' losses as a direct measure is the runner-up: it uses the evidence but skips the differences that could make the airline's likelihood or impact higher or lower.

wrong_explanations.A: It treats the events as evidence, which is right; however, peer losses reflect the peers' own fallbacks and contracts, so the rating needs adjusting for the airline's exposure first.
wrong_explanations.C: Replacing the platform is a response decision for the risk owner, made after the scenario is rated; choosing it from peer news skips the analysis.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for a local loss throws away the best warning available; external events cover failures too rare to have happened inside one airline yet.

tips: Eliminate: C picks a response before the scenario is rated, and D sets aside external evidence because the airline has not suffered the loss itself.
Final two: B beats A because external events inform the rating only after adjusting for the airline's own exposure; using peer losses unadjusted imports their circumstances.
Exam cue: external loss data is evidence, not a verdict. Use it in the rating, scaled to the enterprise's own exposure and controls.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Repeated small AI errors
questions.question: A broadband provider's AI billing assistant applied the wrong tariff to 300 customer bills last quarter; the service desk closed each as a separate ticket after correcting it. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Escalate the AI scenario to the board as an incident
options.B: Confirm each customer received a corrected bill
options.C: Assess whether each ticket met its service target
options.D: Assess the errors' combined impact on the AI scenario

questions.key_concept: Many small AI errors closed one by one can add up to a significant risk event; aggregate them and assess their combined impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice how the errors were handled.
questions.correct_explanation: Each ticket was closed as a service issue, so nobody has measured what 300 billing errors mean together: overcharged customers, complaints and regulatory exposure. Aggregating them and assessing the combined impact on the AI billing scenario comes first, so the business owner can decide on a response. Escalating to the board is the runner-up: the errors may prove significant, but escalation before analysis gives the board a count, not an impact.

wrong_explanations.A: The board may need to hear of it; however, escalating 300 closed tickets before their combined impact is assessed reports a number, not a risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Confirming corrected bills checks the customer fix one account at a time; it does not measure what the pattern means for the business.
wrong_explanations.C: Ticket service times measure service desk performance; they say nothing about the business harm that 300 wrong bills caused.

tips: Eliminate: B and C look at bills and tickets one by one, which is how the risk was missed.
Final two: D beats A because the combined impact must be analyzed before it is escalated; the board needs an impact, not a ticket count.
Exam cue: repeated small AI errors can be one significant risk event in aggregate. Closing each ticket is not closing the risk.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Elements of a fraud scenario
questions.question: A risk analyst is drafting a fraud scenario for a bank's payment API. Which of the following MOST accurately describes the scenario's threat event?

options.A: Replay of stolen session tokens against the API
options.B: Session tokens that stay valid after users sign out
options.C: An organized fraud group targeting banks
options.D: Losses from payments sent to mule accounts

questions.key_concept: A threat event is what a threat source does; keep it separate from the source, the vulnerability it uses and the impact it causes.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option into who acts, what happens, which weakness is used and what harm follows.
questions.correct_explanation: In a risk scenario, the threat event is the action the threat source carries out; here, replaying stolen session tokens against the API. The fraud group is the threat source, the runner-up, because it names who acts rather than what they do. Keeping source, event, vulnerability and impact separate lets the analyst gather the right likelihood evidence for each and match controls to the weakness.

wrong_explanations.B: Tokens that stay valid after sign-out are a vulnerability, the weakness the event exploits; recording a weakness as the threat is a classic scenario error.
wrong_explanations.C: The fraud group is the threat source. It belongs in the scenario, but it is the actor, not the event it carries out.
wrong_explanations.D: Losses from payments sent to mule accounts are the business impact, the consequence that follows the event.

tips: Eliminate: B is the vulnerability the attack uses, and D is the business impact that follows it.
Final two: A beats C because a threat event is the action; the fraud group is the source that carries it out.
Exam cue: in a scenario, separate who acts (source), what they do (event), the weakness used (vulnerability) and the harm (impact).

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Threat analysis for a new connection
questions.question: A manufacturer plans to connect its plant-floor controllers to a cloud analytics service, and the security team offers its threat intelligence feed as the project's threat analysis. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Filter the feed for alerts on the controllers' vendor
options.B: Rate the project's risk on the feed's sector threat level
options.C: Model how the new connection could be attacked or fail
options.D: Ask the plant director to accept the connection's risk

questions.key_concept: Threat intelligence is an input to analysis, not the analysis; a new design needs a threat model of how it could be attacked or fail.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is new in the plant's design and what the security team is offering.
questions.correct_explanation: A feed reports what attackers are doing across many organizations; it cannot show how this particular link between controllers and a cloud service could be attacked or fail. Modeling the new design, for example with STRIDE or attack trees, finds those paths, and relevant intelligence then shows which are credible. Filtering the feed is the runner-up: useful input, but it covers only reported vendor threats, not the design's own weaknesses.

wrong_explanations.A: Relevant alerts are a useful input; however, they cover only threats already reported for the vendor, not the new paths this connection itself creates.
wrong_explanations.B: A sector-wide threat level is not the project's risk; the rating needs this design's attack paths, vulnerabilities and business impact.
wrong_explanations.D: Acceptance belongs to the risk owner after analysis; asking for it before any threat analysis gives the director nothing to base the decision on.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a sector threat level as the project's risk rating, and D seeks acceptance before any analysis exists.
Final two: C beats A because a threat model covers how this design could fail; feed alerts only add evidence about threats already reported.
Exam cue: intelligence feeds inform threat analysis but never replace it. A new design gets a threat model, with intelligence used to judge which paths are credible.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Public access to a pricing model
questions.question: An insurer plans to let brokers query its machine-learning pricing model through an internet API that returns exact premiums. Which of the following AI-specific threats is MOST relevant for the risk practitioner to record?

options.A: Poisoning of the model's historical training data
options.B: Indirect prompt injection through broker emails
options.C: Denial of service against the pricing interface
options.D: Model extraction through large volumes of price queries

questions.key_concept: Query access alone can let an attacker rebuild a model; exposing exact outputs through a public API makes model extraction the leading AI threat.
questions.pre_read: Notice what an outsider can reach through the API and what it returns.
questions.correct_explanation: Model extraction needs only the ability to send queries and read outputs, which this API gives every broker, and exact premiums make each answer more revealing. Repeated queries could let a competitor rebuild a functionally equivalent pricing model, so the risk practitioner records it as a scenario for the pricing owner. Poisoning is the runner-up: a real AI threat, but it needs access to the training data pipeline, which a query-only API does not give.

wrong_explanations.A: Poisoning is a major AI threat; however, it works through the training data pipeline, and a query-only API gives brokers no route into that data.
wrong_explanations.B: Indirect prompt injection targets models that read untrusted text, such as language assistants; a pricing model scoring application data reads no broker emails.
wrong_explanations.C: Denial of service is a real threat to any public interface, but it is not specific to AI and belongs in the general service scenario.

tips: Eliminate: B targets language models that read untrusted text, and C is a general availability threat, not one specific to AI.
Final two: D beats A because query access alone enables extraction, while poisoning needs a route into the training data that this API does not offer.
Exam cue: match the AI threat to the access the attacker has: queries enable extraction and inversion, data pipelines enable poisoning, untrusted text enables prompt injection.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Clean scan results
questions.question: A retailer's IT director tells the risk committee that the company's overall vulnerability exposure is low because monthly scans of all systems find no critical issues. What is the GREATEST weakness in this conclusion?

options.A: Flaws disclosed between monthly scans go unseen
options.B: Scans cannot find people or process weaknesses
options.C: The scans are run by the team that applies patches
options.D: Monthly results are not reported as a trend

questions.key_concept: Vulnerability scans see only technical flaws; people and process weaknesses, such as missing approvals or untrained staff, also expose the business.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the director's conclusion rests on.
questions.correct_explanation: A clean scan says only that known technical flaws were not found on the systems scanned. Weak approvals, poor segregation of duties, untrained staff and untested recovery plans never show up in a scan, yet they expose the retailer as much as a missing patch. The gap between scans is the runner-up: it is a real limitation, but it narrows the technical picture, while the director's conclusion leaves out whole categories of weakness.

wrong_explanations.A: A month between scans leaves new flaws unseen for a while; however, this narrows a technical view rather than missing whole categories of weakness.
wrong_explanations.C: Scanning by the patching team is normal first-line practice; who runs the scan does not change which kinds of weakness it can detect.
wrong_explanations.D: A trend would improve the report's presentation, but it would still describe only the technical flaws a scanner detects.

tips: Eliminate: C raises who runs the scans, not what they miss, and D changes how results are presented rather than what they cover.
Final two: B beats A because the director's conclusion leaves out whole classes of weakness; the gap between scans only delays finding technical flaws.
Exam cue: vulnerabilities live in people, process and technology. When two weaknesses are both real, GREATEST picks the one that leaves the most exposure unseen.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Choosing the first fix
questions.question: Which of the following findings, shown with their CVSS Base scores, should a cinema chain's risk practitioner recommend fixing FIRST?

options.A: A 6.8 flaw under active attack on the booking site
options.B: A 7.5 flaw under active attack on an office printer
options.C: An 8.2 flaw with no known exploit in the HR system
options.D: A 9.1 flaw with no known exploit on the intranet

questions.key_concept: Fix order follows business risk: active exploitation, reachability and the asset's business value can outweigh a higher severity score.
questions.pre_read: Read each finding's details, not just its score.
questions.correct_explanation: Two flaws are already under attack, so their likelihood is highest, and the choice between them turns on business impact. The booking site earns the cinema chain's revenue and serves customers online, so it ranks first despite the lowest score. The printer flaw is the runner-up: it is under attack too, but an office printer supports little of the business. CVSS rates a flaw's severity; the practitioner ranks fixes by risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Active attack makes this flaw urgent too; however, an office printer supports little of the business, so the same exploitation threatens far less than on the booking site.
wrong_explanations.C: The HR system's data is sensitive and the score higher; however, with no known exploit it is less likely to be hit soon than a flaw already under active attack.
wrong_explanations.D: The highest score tempts, but with no known exploit on an internal intranet, its likelihood today is lower than that of the flaws under attack.

tips: Eliminate: C and D rank by score alone; neither flaw has a known exploit, so both are less likely to be hit soon than the two under attack.
Final two: A beats B because both are under attack, and the booking site carries the chain's revenue and customers; the printer supports little of the business.
Exam cue: CVSS is one input. Rank fixes by business risk: exploitation in the wild, reachability and the asset's value to the business.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Site in a flood zone
questions.question: A logistics firm's main data center sits in a mapped flood zone, though the site has never flooded. How should the risk analyst BEST reflect the location in the data center outage scenario?

options.A: As the environmental threat source in the scenario
options.B: As a factor raising the cost of each outage
options.C: As a condition raising the scenario's likelihood
options.D: As no factor until the site has had a flood

questions.key_concept: A predisposing condition, such as a site in a flood zone, raises the likelihood that a threat event causes harm even when nothing is broken.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of the scenario the site's location actually changes.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-30 gives a facility in a flood-prone region as an example of a predisposing condition: the location does not act, but it raises the likelihood that a flood disrupts the data center. The analyst therefore reflects it in the scenario's likelihood. Calling the location the threat source is the runner-up: the flood itself is the environmental threat, while the location is the condition that makes it more likely to cause harm.

wrong_explanations.A: The flood is the environmental threat; the site's location does not act on the data center, it changes how likely a flood is to disrupt it.
wrong_explanations.B: The cost of an outage depends on the business processes the data center supports, not on where the building stands.
wrong_explanations.D: No flood so far does not make one unlikely; the mapped flood zone is direct evidence that the chance of flooding is higher here.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses likelihood with the cost of an outage, and D treats a clean history as proof that a flood is unlikely.
Final two: C beats A because the flood is the threat, while the location is a predisposing condition that makes the flood more likely to cause harm.
Exam cue: weaknesses are not only broken things. Conditions such as location or a single shared supplier raise likelihood and belong in the scenario rating.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Tabletop exercise participants
questions.question: A risk practitioner is planning a tabletop exercise on a ransomware scenario at a food distributor. Which of the following participants is MOST important to include?

options.A: Owners of the processes the attack would halt
options.B: Control owners responsible for backup and recovery
options.C: Internal auditors who will assess the exercise results
options.D: An external negotiator experienced in ransom demands

questions.key_concept: A tabletop exercise tests a scenario and its responses with the people who make the business decisions, so the affected process owners must take part.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a tabletop exercise is meant to test before choosing who must attend.
questions.correct_explanation: A tabletop is a discussion-based walkthrough that tests roles, coordination and decisions against a scenario. The decisions that matter in ransomware, such as which deliveries to stop, what to tell customers and when to switch to manual work, belong to the owners of the affected processes, so their presence matters most. Backup control owners are the runner-up: they matter for recovery steps, but cannot make the business calls the exercise is testing.

wrong_explanations.B: Backup control owners add recovery detail; however, without the process owners, the exercise cannot test the business decisions a ransomware attack forces.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance and may review the results later; as participants, auditors would not make the response decisions being tested.
wrong_explanations.D: A negotiator is a specialist the distributor might call during a real attack; the exercise first needs the people who own the business decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C brings the third line into management's exercise as a participant, and D adds a specialist before the people who own the decisions.
Final two: A beats B because the business decisions belong to process owners; control owners explain recovery steps but cannot make those calls.
Exam cue: tabletop exercises test decisions as much as technology. The people who own the business impact must be in the room.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Gap found in an exercise
questions.question: During a tabletop exercise, a bank's payments team cannot agree who may approve shutting down instant payments during a cyberattack. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response to this finding?

options.A: Note the finding in the report for next year's exercise
options.B: Name the security operations lead as the decision owner
options.C: Rerun the exercise until the team agrees on an approver
options.D: Log a tracked action with an owner and a due date

questions.key_concept: Gaps found in a tabletop exercise become tracked actions with an accountable owner and a date, not notes kept for the next exercise.
questions.pre_read: Notice what kind of gap the exercise found.
questions.correct_explanation: The exercise exposed a real gap: in an attack, nobody knows who can stop instant payments, and delay could increase losses. Its value comes from closing that gap, so the finding becomes a tracked action with an accountable owner and due date, such as the payments head working with senior management to set decision rights. Recording it in the report is the runner-up: it documents the gap but leaves it open until next year.

wrong_explanations.A: Recording the finding preserves it; however, with no owner or date, the bank could face a real attack with the same gap for a year.
wrong_explanations.B: Decision rights over a payments shutdown are set by the business and senior management; the practitioner does not assign them to the security team.
wrong_explanations.C: Repeating the exercise tests the same gap again; agreement under exercise pressure is not a defined, approved decision right.

tips: Eliminate: B has the practitioner assign a business decision right, and C repeats the exercise instead of fixing what it found.
Final two: D beats A because a finding without an owner and a date stays open; a tracked action gets the gap closed before a real attack.
Exam cue: an exercise is only as useful as its follow-up. Every gap becomes an owned, dated action, tracked like any other risk action.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Too many scenarios
questions.question: An energy retailer's risk team has logged 210 IT risk scenarios, and risk owners say they cannot review them before the annual rating cycle. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT rate the scenarios it ranks as most severe
options.B: Merge overlapping scenarios under the company's objectives
options.C: Review the 210 against objectives over two cycles
options.D: Replace them with the twelve scenarios in a vendor library

questions.key_concept: A scenario set must be small enough for owners to manage; merge overlapping scenarios under the business objectives they threaten.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the owners cannot cope with the set as it stands.
questions.correct_explanation: Two hundred scenarios cannot be reviewed meaningfully, and many will overlap. Anchoring the set on business objectives and merging technical scenarios beneath them keeps every real exposure visible in a number owners can rate. Swapping in a vendor library is the runner-up: it shrinks the list quickly, but generic scenarios are not tailored to the retailer's own processes and would drop risks the team has already identified.

wrong_explanations.A: Letting IT pick the scenarios ranks risk by technical judgment alone; the business owners who bear the impact would never see the rest.
wrong_explanations.C: Stretching reviews over two cycles leaves half the scenarios unreviewed for a year and does nothing about overlap in the set.
wrong_explanations.D: A library is a useful starting point; however, replacing the retailer's own scenarios with generic ones loses the risks specific to its business.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the business out of choosing which risks matter, and C keeps an unmanageable set and delays half the reviews.
Final two: B beats D because merging keeps the retailer's own risks while shrinking the set; a generic library is a starting point, not a substitute.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Ratings that disagree
questions.question: Two analysts at a telecom rate the same outage scenario's likelihood as possible and likely; the first had the next year in mind, the second the next five. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Average the two likelihood ratings into one level
options.B: Use the higher rating as the prudent choice
options.C: Set one time frame for all likelihood ratings
options.D: Ask the risk owner to choose between the ratings

questions.key_concept: Likelihood only has meaning over a stated time frame; ratings made over different periods cannot be compared or combined.
questions.pre_read: Look for why the two ratings differ before deciding which one to keep.
questions.correct_explanation: The analysts did not disagree about the scenario; they rated likelihood over different periods, and an event is naturally more likely over five years than over one. Setting one time frame for all likelihood ratings removes the cause, after which the scenario is re-rated consistently. Asking the risk owner to choose is the runner-up: the owner agrees the final rating, but choosing between two incomparable ratings leaves the cause in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Averaging two ratings made over different periods produces a level that matches neither, and the next pair of analysts would diverge again.
wrong_explanations.B: Choosing the higher rating looks cautious, but it rests on a five-year horizon that other scenarios in the register may not use.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner agrees the final rating; however, choosing between ratings built on different time frames leaves the inconsistency that caused the gap.

tips: Eliminate: A blends two incomparable ratings, and B keeps the higher one without fixing why they differ.
Final two: C beats D because the ratings differ only in time frame; fix the basis first, then the owner can agree a rating made on it.
Exam cue: likelihood is always over a stated period. When ratings disagree, check the basis (time frame, scale, level definitions) before choosing a rating.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Results before a launch
questions.question: A week before a retailer launches a mobile app, the risk practitioner completes its risk assessment, which rates two scenarios above appetite. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Add both scenarios to the register for the annual review
options.B: Ask the app's control owners to fix both weaknesses
options.C: Recommend postponing the launch until both are mitigated
options.D: Take the results to the app's risk owner before launch

questions.key_concept: An assessment is complete only when decision makers have its results in time to act; above-appetite findings go to the risk owner first.
questions.pre_read: Notice the deadline and where the results are now.
questions.correct_explanation: Results that nobody with authority has seen cannot inform the launch decision. With two scenarios above appetite and a week to go, the practitioner first gives the results to the app's risk owner, who chooses among responses such as mitigating, transferring or delaying. Recommending a postponement is the runner-up: delay may be the right call, but pushing one response before the owner has seen the analysis narrows a decision that belongs to the owner.

wrong_explanations.A: The register should hold the scenarios, but waiting for the annual review means the launch decision is made without the results.
wrong_explanations.B: Fixing weaknesses is one possible response; asking control owners to start before the risk owner chooses a response acts ahead of the decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Postponement may turn out to be right; however, the risk owner should see the results and the options before one response is pushed.

tips: Eliminate: A holds the results until after the launch decision, and B starts a treatment before the risk owner has chosen one.
Final two: D beats C because the owner must see the results and decide; recommending one response first narrows a choice that is not the practitioner's.
Exam cue: an assessment is not finished until the people who decide have its results in time to act on them.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Tolerable data loss
questions.question: The sales director of an events ticketing firm tells the risk practitioner that losing more than one hour of ticket sales records would be unacceptable. How should the practitioner BEST record this in the BIA?

options.A: A one-hour recovery point objective for ticket sales
options.B: A one-hour recovery time objective for ticket sales
options.C: A one-year retention period for sales backups
options.D: A one-hour maximum tolerable outage for ticket sales

questions.key_concept: A limit on tolerable data loss is recorded as the RPO; time to recover is the RTO, and the longest tolerable disruption is the MTO.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly what the director says would be unacceptable.
questions.correct_explanation: The director has limited lost data, not downtime: no more than one hour of sales records may be lost. That is a recovery point objective, so the BIA records a one-hour RPO for sales records, and IT designs backup or replication to meet it. A one-hour RTO is the runner-up: it limits how long recovery takes, yet a fast restore can still bring back data that is a day old.

wrong_explanations.B: An RTO limits how long recovery may take; however, the director limited lost data, and a fast restore can still bring back data that is a day old.
wrong_explanations.C: A retention period sets how long backup copies are kept; it does not limit how many hours of recent sales records can be lost.
wrong_explanations.D: The MTO is the longest disruption the business can tolerate; the director limited lost records, not how long ticket sales can stop.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses how long backups are kept with how much data can be lost, and D turns a data-loss limit into an outage limit.
Final two: A beats B because the director's limit is on lost data, which is the RPO; an RTO limits recovery time and can still bring back day-old data.
Exam cue: RPO is how much data you can lose, which sets copy frequency; RTO is how long you can wait. Set and check each separately.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Recovery time beyond the outage limit
questions.question: A distributor's BIA sets a 24-hour maximum tolerable outage for order processing, but IT's tested recovery plan restores the order system in 36 hours. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Extend the order process's MTO to 36 hours in the BIA
options.B: Report the gap to the owner of order processing
options.C: Ask the recovery control owner to buy a faster service
options.D: Record the RTO as 36 hours to match IT's capability

questions.key_concept: An RTO must fit inside the maximum tolerable outage; when recovery cannot meet it, the process owner decides how to close the gap.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the business can tolerate with what IT can deliver before choosing a step.
questions.correct_explanation: The business can tolerate 24 hours without order processing, but tested recovery takes 36, so a real outage would cause unacceptable harm. Closing the gap costs money, so the order-processing owner, whose tolerance the BIA records, weighs faster recovery against the impact. Buying a faster service is the runner-up: it may be the answer, but committing spend before the owner weighs the options takes the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: The MTO reflects how long the business can survive the outage; stretching it to match IT's recovery time hides the harm instead of reducing it.
wrong_explanations.C: A faster service may close the gap; however, the owner should weigh its cost against the BIA impact before anyone commits the spend.
wrong_explanations.D: Recovery objectives come from business tolerance, not from what IT can deliver today; recording 36 hours accepts a gap the business never agreed to.

tips: Eliminate: A bends the business tolerance to fit IT, and D sets the RTO from IT's capability instead of the BIA.
Final two: B beats C because the owner whose tolerance is breached decides how to close the gap; buying a service first spends money the owner has not weighed.
Exam cue: the RTO must sit inside the MTO. When recovery cannot meet it, take the gap to the business owner rather than changing the numbers or buying a fix.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Missing AI service dependency
questions.question: A city's permit office relies on a vendor's AI service to read permit applications, but its BIA lists only the permit database as a dependency. What is the GREATEST risk of leaving the BIA unchanged?

options.A: The vendor's own continuity plan would go unreviewed
options.B: The AI service's failure rate would go unmeasured
options.C: Recovery plans would omit a resource the process needs
options.D: Drift in the AI model's accuracy would go unnoticed

questions.key_concept: A BIA that omits a dependency leaves that resource out of recovery planning.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the BIA is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA tells recovery planning which resources each critical process needs and how soon. With the AI service missing, no one sets a recovery requirement for it, so continuity plans and the vendor contract may not restore it before applications back up. An unreviewed vendor plan is the runner-up: it matters, but the city can only judge that plan against a requirement the BIA has not yet set.

wrong_explanations.A: Reviewing the vendor's plan matters; however, it can only be judged against a recovery requirement that the BIA has not yet set for the service.
wrong_explanations.B: A failure rate is a likelihood input for the risk assessment; a BIA assumes the disruption happens and measures its impact over time.
wrong_explanations.D: Watching model accuracy is AI performance monitoring; a BIA records dependencies and the impact of losing them, not model drift.

tips: Eliminate: B asks a BIA for likelihood, and D expects it to monitor model accuracy; neither is what a BIA does.
Final two: C beats A because the BIA sets the recovery requirement first; a vendor's plan is only judged against it.
Exam cue: when a process gains a new dependency, especially an AI or cloud service, the BIA must list it, or recovery planning will miss it.
