questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Objective for the alternate site
questions.question: When the risk practitioner records a bank's BIA results, which objective is MOST appropriate for stating how much of normal payment volume branch payments must handle at the alternate site?

options.A: The recovery time objective
options.B: The recovery point objective
options.C: The acceptable interruption window
options.D: The service delivery objective

questions.key_concept: The service delivery objective sets the level of service needed during alternate processing; RTO and AIW are time limits, and RPO limits data loss.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly what the objective must state.
questions.correct_explanation: The service delivery objective (SDO) is the level of service the business needs while it runs in alternate mode, until normal operation is restored. Stating the share of payment volume the alternate site must handle sets that level and drives the site's capacity. The RTO is the runner-up: it sets how soon payments must be running again, not how much service they must deliver once they are.

wrong_explanations.A: The RTO sets how soon payments must be running again after a disruption; however, it says nothing about how much volume the alternate site must then handle.
wrong_explanations.B: The RPO sets how much data loss is tolerable, which drives backup frequency; it does not set a level of service during alternate processing.
wrong_explanations.C: The AIW is the longest a system can be unavailable before objectives suffer; it is a time limit, not the service level required at the alternate site.

tips: Eliminate: B limits data loss, and C limits how long a system can be down; neither sets a service level.
Final two: D beats A because the bank must state how much service runs in alternate mode; the RTO only sets how soon recovery happens.
Exam cue: RTO, MTO and AIW say how soon; RPO says how much data; SDO says how much service while running in alternate mode.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Entries for a retired system
questions.question: A bus operator has retired its old mobile ticketing app, and the IT manager asks the risk analyst to delete the app's four entries from the risk register. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Delete the entries once the IT owner confirms retirement
options.B: Close the entries with the risk owners' approval
options.C: Keep the entries open until the annual register review
options.D: Move the entries to the IT team's operational issue log

questions.key_concept: Register entries are closed, not deleted, with a recorded reason and the risk owner's approval, so the history stays available.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the register's history is for before deciding what happens to the entries.
questions.correct_explanation: Retiring the app may remove the risk, but the register keeps the record: the entries are closed with the reason, such as retirement and data disposal, and the risk owners' approval. That history supports trend analysis, audits and later questions about the app's data. Deleting them once IT confirms retirement is the runner-up: it reflects the change, but erases the record and lets IT make a closure decision that belongs to the owners.

wrong_explanations.A: IT's confirmation is useful evidence; however, deleting erases the risk history, and closing an entry is the risk owner's decision, not IT's.
wrong_explanations.C: Leaving entries open for a system that no longer exists overstates the risk profile until the review, and still needs the owners' decision later.
wrong_explanations.D: An operational issue log is not where enterprise risk is tracked; moving the entries hides their history from risk owners and the risk profile.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps a retired system's risks open as if nothing changed, and D moves risk records out of the register into an IT log.
Final two: B beats A because entries are closed with a reason and the owner's approval, keeping the history; deleting them erases it and lets IT decide.
Exam cue: register entries close on evidence and with the risk owner's approval; they are not simply deleted.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Signs of a current register
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows that an airport operator's IT risk register is being kept current?

options.A: Ratings revised after incidents and failed tests
options.B: Entry reviews held at the annual risk workshop
options.C: Entries closed on the day treatment plans are approved
options.D: A total number of entries that grows each quarter

questions.key_concept: A current register changes when evidence changes: incidents, control test results, audit findings and business changes trigger updates between scheduled reviews.
questions.pre_read: Ask what should make a register entry change, and which option shows that happening.
questions.correct_explanation: A register is current when its ratings follow the evidence: an incident, near miss or failed control test changes likelihood or control effectiveness, so the affected entries are revised promptly. Ratings revised after such events show that link working. The annual workshop is the runner-up: scheduled reviews matter, but on their own they leave the register up to a year behind events.

wrong_explanations.B: Scheduled reviews are part of maintenance; however, a register reviewed only once a year can be months behind the incidents and test failures that change risk.
wrong_explanations.C: An approved plan reduces nothing until it is implemented and working; closing entries on approval makes the register look better than reality.
wrong_explanations.D: A growing count shows that entries are being added, not that existing ratings reflect today's incidents and control results.

tips: Eliminate: C closes entries on approved plans, which reduce nothing yet, and D counts entries instead of checking whether ratings are up to date.
Final two: A beats B because event-driven updates keep ratings current between reviews; an annual review alone can leave them a year out of date.
Exam cue: a current register is evidence-driven. Look for ratings that move when incidents, tests and changes happen, not just on a calendar.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Cost of the top-ranked risks
questions.question: After a qualitative first ranking of 70 IT risk scenarios, a manufacturer's board asks what the top five could cost. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Convert the 70 ratings to costs using scale midpoints
options.B: Explain that the top five ratings cannot show cost
options.C: Estimate loss ranges for the top five scenarios
options.D: Redo the 70 scenarios with quantitative loss models

questions.key_concept: Methods combine: screen many risks qualitatively, then quantify the few top risks where loss data supports a credible figure.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the board is asking for, and about which risks.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's question is about cost, which qualitative levels cannot answer, but it concerns only the top five. Quantifying those five, from loss data and expert ranges with the uncertainty stated, gives the board money figures where they matter. Redoing all 70 quantitatively is the runner-up: it would also produce costs, but at heavy effort, and for most scenarios thin data would make the figures falsely precise.

wrong_explanations.A: Scale midpoints turn ordinal levels into numbers that look exact but were never estimated, giving the board false precision across the whole list.
wrong_explanations.B: The ratings cannot show cost as they stand; however, the board's question can be answered by quantifying the few risks it is asking about.
wrong_explanations.D: Quantitative models need good data and effort; spending them on 70 scenarios, most with thin data, is disproportionate when the board asked about five.

tips: Eliminate: A turns ordinal levels into invented costs, and B declines a question that analysis can answer.
Final two: C beats D because quantitative effort goes only where the board's decision needs it; redoing all 70 adds effort and false precision.
Exam cue: methods combine. Screen many risks qualitatively, then quantify the top few where data supports a credible figure.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Simulated loss against tolerance
questions.question: A marketplace's Monte Carlo fraud run gives yearly losses averaging $300,000, with a 5% chance of exceeding $1,200,000. The board's limit is a 5% chance of exceeding $1,000,000; what is the risk analyst's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Not comparable until rated high, medium or low
options.B: Within tolerance, judged on the $300,000 mean
options.C: Undecidable until the model gives one figure
options.D: Beyond tolerance, judged on the $1,200,000 figure

questions.key_concept: Compare a simulated loss distribution with tolerance as written; a limit on the chance of a large loss is tested on the tail.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each figure from the simulation measures.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's tolerance is a probability: at most a 5% chance of losing over $1,000,000 in a year. The simulation gives a 5% chance of losing more than $1,200,000, so the chance of exceeding $1,000,000 is above 5%: the scenario is beyond tolerance. Judging on the $300,000 mean is the runner-up: it is the expected loss, but a limit on rare large losses is tested against the distribution's tail, not its average.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating the result high, medium or low throws away the probabilities the board's tolerance is written in; the simulation can be compared with it directly.
wrong_explanations.B: The mean is the expected yearly loss; however, the board set its tolerance on the chance of a large loss, which the mean does not show.
wrong_explanations.C: A Monte Carlo result is a distribution by design; asking for a single figure discards the tail information the tolerance needs.

tips: Eliminate: A and C refuse to compare, yet the simulation's probabilities match the way the tolerance is written.
Final two: D beats B because the tolerance limits the chance of a large loss; the mean says nothing about the tail.
Exam cue: compare a simulated loss distribution with a limit in the form the limit is written; a probability limit is tested on the tail, not the average.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Equal scores on a matrix
questions.question: On a bank's risk matrix, card skimming (40 small losses a year) and a week-long banking outage (once in 20 years) both score 10. How should the risk analyst BEST present them to the committee?

options.A: With likelihood and impact shown for each scenario
options.B: As equal-priority scenarios with the same score
options.C: With the outage ranked higher for its larger impact
options.D: With each score converted to an annual loss figure

questions.key_concept: A combined matrix score shows order, not the shape of a risk; equal scores can hide very different likelihood and impact that need different responses.
questions.pre_read: Notice how each scenario reaches its score of 10.
questions.correct_explanation: The equal scores hide two different risks: about 40 small skimming losses a year call for mitigating controls, while a severe outage expected once in 20 years may call for continuity planning or transfer. Showing likelihood and impact separately lets the committee see that difference. Treating them as equal priorities is the runner-up: the matrix does rank them equally, but the score is ordinal and the decision needs the shape behind it.

wrong_explanations.B: The shared score is a fair ranking signal; however, it hides whether the risk comes from frequency or severity, which the committee needs to choose responses.
wrong_explanations.C: Ranking on impact alone drops likelihood, so the frequent skimming losses would be undervalued however often they occur.
wrong_explanations.D: Converting ordinal matrix scores into money produces precise-looking numbers the data does not support, adding false precision instead of clarity.

tips: Eliminate: C ranks on one dimension only, and D turns ordinal scores into invented money figures.
Final two: A beats B because equal scores can hide opposite risk profiles; showing both dimensions gives the committee what it needs to choose different responses.
Exam cue: matrix scores are ordinal. When the decision depends on how a risk arises, report likelihood and impact, not just the combined score.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Expected loss from outage history
questions.question: Each outage of a parcel firm's sorting system costs about $120,000, and the system has failed three times in the past six years. What is the risk analyst's BEST estimate of the annualized loss expectancy?

options.A: About $20,000 a year
options.B: About $40,000 a year
options.C: About $60,000 a year
options.D: About $360,000 a year

questions.key_concept: ALE equals single loss expectancy times annual rate of occurrence; three events in six years is an ARO of 0.5.
questions.pre_read: Identify each part of the ALE formula from the stem before choosing a figure.
questions.correct_explanation: The SLE is $120,000, the cost of one outage. Three outages in six years is an ARO of 0.5, half an outage a year, so the ALE is $120,000 times 0.5, about $60,000 a year. The $20,000 figure is the runner-up: it treats the six-year window as one outage every six years, missing that three occurred. An ALE is only as good as this history, so its source is stated.

wrong_explanations.A: This treats the rate as one outage every six years; three outages in six years is an ARO of 0.5, not about 0.17.
wrong_explanations.B: This divides the cost by the number of outages; ALE multiplies the cost of one outage by how many occur each year.
wrong_explanations.D: This is the total loss over all six years, not the expected loss in one year.

tips: Eliminate: B divides the cost by the number of outages, and D gives the six-year total instead of a yearly figure.
Final two: C beats A because three outages in six years is an ARO of 0.5; A uses one outage in six years.
Exam cue: convert history to an annual rate first (events divided by years), then multiply the single loss by that rate.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Large gap from one control
questions.question: An online game publisher's account takeover scenario has very high inherent risk but low current risk, almost entirely because of one bot-detection control. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Lowering the inherent rating to match current risk
options.B: Regular testing of the bot-detection control
options.C: A KRI on the volume of account takeover attempts
options.D: Raising current risk to reflect the reliance

questions.key_concept: A wide gap between inherent and current risk marks reliance on a key control, so that control's continued effectiveness needs regular evidence.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the low current rating comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: Low current risk here rests almost entirely on one control, so if bot detection weakens, the risk jumps back toward its very high inherent level. Regular testing, backed by key control indicators, shows whether the control still works and keeps the current rating honest. A KRI on attempt volume is the runner-up: it tracks the threat, but steady or rising attempts say nothing about whether the control is still stopping them.

wrong_explanations.A: Inherent risk is rated before controls, so it does not fall because a control works; changing it would hide how much the scenario depends on that control.
wrong_explanations.C: Attempt volume is a useful threat signal; however, it cannot show whether the single control holding the risk down is still working.
wrong_explanations.D: Reliance on one control is a concentration to watch, not a reason to re-rate; current risk reflects how well the control works today, which only testing shows.

tips: Eliminate: A lowers inherent risk because of a control, which inherent risk does not count, and D re-rates the risk for reliance instead of checking whether the control still works.
Final two: B beats C because the current rating is only as good as the control behind it; attempt volume tracks the threat, not the control.
Exam cue: high inherent and low current risk means a key control. Make sure there is regular evidence that it keeps working.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Paper for a tolerance breach
questions.question: Failed access reviews push a pension fund's member-data scenario beyond the executive committee's tolerance; the risk owner asks the committee to accept it for a quarter. What MOST belongs in the risk practitioner's committee paper?

options.A: The owner's case for exceeding the tolerance
options.B: The cost of an automated access review tool
options.C: The count of access reviews failed this year
options.D: Current risk set against the breached tolerance

questions.key_concept: A request to accept a tolerance breach goes to the limit-setter with the current risk measured against that limit.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the committee is being asked to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee is asked to accept a risk above a limit it set, so the paper must show how far current risk now sits beyond that tolerance and what that means for the fund. The committee can then weigh the owner's request on the facts. The owner's case is the runner-up: the committee should hear it, but without current risk set against the tolerance it cannot judge what it is being asked to accept.

wrong_explanations.A: The owner's reasons belong in the paper; however, they cannot show the committee how far beyond its own limit the risk now sits.
wrong_explanations.B: A tool's cost informs treatment options; it does not tell the committee how much risk it is being asked to accept for the quarter.
wrong_explanations.C: The failed reviews are the cause; a count of them does not translate into exposure measured against the tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: B prices one treatment and C counts the cause; neither shows the exposure the committee is asked to accept.
Final two: D beats A because acceptance beyond tolerance turns on how far the risk exceeds the limit; the owner's case cannot show that.
Exam cue: when a limit-setter is asked to accept a breach, lead with the current risk measured against the limit it set.
